content: The review process was finalized, and feedback was provided to the data user. Alternatively, the date when the dataset was either returned to the CDC or destroyed was documented. The CDC’s re-release of state-provided data as Public-Use Data Sets (PUDS) does not necessitate the use of a Data Sharing Agreement (DSA). When PUDS are created by CDC programs, they should be made accessible to all interested users without any restrictions. Guideline 8: Planning for the Release of Public-Use Data Refer to the CDC/ATSDR Policy on Releasing and Sharing Data for detailed information regarding the release of data for public use. This policy specifies that procedures for releasing public-use data must align with the functions and specifications of the CDC’s Public Health Information Network. The CDC/ATSDR Policy outlines that each plan for releasing public-use data must include the following components: A procedure to ensure that confidential information is not disclosed. A procedure to ensure that the data is released in a format that does not compromise national security or interfere with law enforcement activities. Analysis plans and other documentation required by the Office of Management and Budget regulations on data quality. Instructions for non-CDC users on the appropriate use of the data. The date when the data will be released, which should occur as soon as possible after the data has been collected, reviewed for errors, and validated. The release of these data should not exceed one year after these activities are completed. Best Practices for Guideline 9: The CDC National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) requests that users of PUDS agree to use the data solely for statistical reporting and analysis purposes. Best Practices for Guideline 10: Examples of best practices include: Written requests for access to state-provided data must be submitted on official letterhead. Oral or email requests from a known individual are considered valid without requiring further verification. Electronic authentication protocols may involve methods such as USB connections, digital fobs (auto-generated pass numbers), or smart cards with biometric scans. The electronic identification-authentication process can be linked to authorization rights, which define levels of access. Guideline 11: Requirements for Requestors of Restricted-Access Data All individuals requesting access to restricted-access data are required to sign a Data Sharing Agreement (DSA). The CDC program must confirm, via a statement of response, that the state has granted permission for the data to be re-released as a restricted-access data file. Before the CDC re-releases these data, all requestors must sign a DSA, which governs the protection and use of the data. The CDC program responsible for re-releasing state-provided data will retain signed copies of the DSA. A DSA may also be incorporated into a larger interagency Memorandum of Understanding (MOU). Best Practices for Guideline 11: The 2002 modification to the HIPAA Privacy Rule allows for the release of a limited data set as long as there is a written data use agreement in place. This HIPAA standard aligns with the use of restricted-access data and DSAs as described in the guidelines section of this report.
